newsitem.title: GERMANY: FEATURE - Builders flock to Berlin to help realise dream city.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Builders flock to Berlin to help realise dream city.

text.p: Seven years ago the two halves of Berlin were set to be rejoined across the broken Wall, but look at the city now and it seems as if its heart has been torn out.

Potsdamer Platz, a city square which was once Europe's busiest intersection with traffic heading across the continent from Paris to St Petersburg before the Wall split it, is now a great gaping hole, and the biggest building site in Europe.
Filling that hole and many other city sites is a small army of foreign construction workers from Britain, Ireland, Italy, Portugal and eastern Europe.
Cherished by employers for their hard work, they are loathed by unemployed local German construction workers, whom they are pricing out of the job market.
Twenty thousand German construction workers are unemployed while around 50,000 to 60,000 workers from across Europe have flooded Berlin's sites.

Bricklayers, carpenters and tradesmen have flocked here in what has been described as the new "gold rush" and are prepared to work in all weathers and at weekends to get the job done. Not for them the "bad weather allowance" paid to registered native workers who don't leave the canteen if it gets too cold.

Some have been at the hard end of local feelings -- one group of Italians were badly beaten in a city suburb and fled back to Naples. Shortly afterwards a German newspaper article referred to the foreign workers as "a new kind of slave".
Few speak any German and their English or Italian banter fills local pubs.

They may not be well-liked by the locals but they are vital if Berlin is to realise its dream of creating a new European city complete with new transport infrastructure and real estate designed by world-famous architects for the new millenium.
Some 8-10,000 have come from Britain and Ireland alone. They heard about the jobs in the pubs back home and left families, wives and girlfriends to come and make a fast buck.

Barney, a 37-year-old steel fitter from Inverness in northern Scotland, is typical, though undoubtedly one of the better paid workers. He says he makes 4,000 marks ($2,700) a week "but you probably wouldn't believe me". In Scotland he would make 2-300 pounds ($300-450) a week.
"I'm having the time of my life," he said while nursing a pint of beer with his workmates in one of Berlin's many Irish bars.
Barney, Seamus and Noel don't care if German builders are out of work. "They couldn't do what I do," says Barney. "I work for as long as it takes -- they wouldn't even break sweat."

The German construction industry is governed by strict regulations and though a Scotsman's wage packet might be fatter than that of a native, illegal foreigners still come far cheaper for their employers.

They are paid in cash, by the hour, and employers ignore such conventions as social security contributions. They work more than 60 hours a week, including Saturdays, something the highly-unionised Germans would never dream of.
Seamus from Tipperary in the Irish Republic is a "subby", or sub-contracter, and picks his men up by word of mouth in Berlin's Irish pubs such as the Oscar Wilde or the Kilkenny.

"I pay them their wages, I don't rip them off, but I don't pay any social security or insurance," he says in a thick Irish brogue. Seamus's men earn 30 marks ($20) an hour compared to the 16-20 marks ($11-15) he would give a German worker. "But it's still much cheaper for me," he says, adding that he couldn't employ Germans if he wanted to because he is not legal.
Many of the east European workers are paid as little as five marks an hour, undercutting German levels by far.

The rebuilding of Berlin is a mammoth project -- the city skyline is no longer topped by the dome of the New Synagogue or the Prussian victory column. Instead it has become a forest of cranes swooping silently across the horizon.
Where Potsdamer Platz once stood is now a great hole filled with muddy water and men crawling over a giant-sized sand pit in hard hats. The surrounding streets are a sea of mud.

Many of the foreigners have been ripped off shortly after arriving in the city. One Irish "subbie" is said to prey on new arrivals and make them work for a few weeks without pay, and then looks for new blood once the lads inevitably move on.
Barney said he lost five weeks' wages after arriving in Berlin. "But it would cost thousands to get a solicitor and try to get it back. It's not worth it."

Seamus dismissed the Germans as lazy and Barney's theory is that all Germans who leave school without qualifications are classed as construction workers, are unquailified and unskilled and couldn't do the job even if they tried.

"Of course the foreigners are cheaper," Werner Koehler of the German construction workers union IG Bau told Reuters. They are not covered by wage laws, the employers do not pay any social security and their home countries don't make any social contributions either, he added.
One big construction firm working in Potsdamer Platz admits to using sub-contracters, but when pressed on what type of labour these sub-contracters employ gave a firm "no comment".
Koehler says of the foreign labourers: "Every employee from the EU can come here but they must be governed by the same conditions as German workers."

IG Bau and employers agreed a minimum wage for the industry on Monday after months of dispute. The deal is an attempt to prevent foreign workers undercutting German wages, but will have little weight against thousands of unregistered workers.
Many would say Koehler is fighting a losing battle.

At stake is a high-cost, high-prestige project and Berlin knows it cannot afford to let the work overrun if it is to take its place as a newly-revived European capital and seat of government at the turn of the century.
Berlin's mayor Eberhard Diepgen put it thus: "At Potsdamer Platz, Berlin's dead heart will be resuscitated over the next few years and arise as a pulsing, bubbling centre for the 21st century."
